source.version_note: Journal on Multimodal User Interfaces 15(2), 201–214; online 21 January 2021, June 2021 issue. DOI suffix 020 and November 2020 acceptance are not conflicting publication years.
source.verification_method: All fourteen supplied pages, four figures, four tables, complete scale appendix and 66 references read. Publisher/Crossref verify identity and dates. A targeted source-identity check repairs one garbled author name. No separate supplement/data archive was found in the inspected publisher page; no raw participants, IAGO implementation, saved analysis output or original code obtained.

citation.title: Comparing mind perception in strategic exchanges: human-agent negotiation, dictator and ultimatum games

reading.source_scope_note: Two MTurk studies examine human allocations and negotiation with described or scripted machine agents. Cognitive/affective descriptions, dialogs and expressions are manipulated; the studies do not establish genuine machine emotion or independently measure higher-order mentalizing over time.
access_limits: All main text, four figures, four tables and the complete appendix of mind, standing and IOS items read. Figure 3 standardizes unlike game outcomes; it is not a common monetary effect or a formal cross-task interaction test.

No separate supplementary information or data-availability section was found in the inspected publisher page. The embedded appendix was read; this does not establish that no data or other materials exist elsewhere.

No participant-level records, negotiation platform implementation, randomization/exclusion log, preregistration or original statistical output obtained. No reanalysis or source code execution performed.

The earlier conference paper cited at reference 54 and original IOS, theory-of-mind and negotiation sources were not independently fully read. An incomplete bibliography search stopped after a rate limit; no guessed metadata result was substituted. Cited books are not claimed read.

study.study_1_sample: 202 MTurk participants, 131 men, 70 women and one undisclosed gender. Described cognitive ability × affective capacity is randomly assigned. All participants complete dictator game first, then ultimatum game; game order is fixed, not randomized. These are 202 people’s two allocations rather than 404 independent participants.
study.study_1_incentive: Participants distribute 20 lottery tickets and receive $1.80; one randomly chosen participant receives an additional $10. Lottery participation and point allocation are behavioral choices, but not direct observed cash transfers to a sentient robot or full evidence of moral motivation.
study.manipulation: Descriptions distinguish thinking/reasoning and emotional experience. The manipulations are not psychologically orthogonal: both assigned factors affect perceived agency, and in Study 1 both affect perceived patiency. The source acknowledges correlations and retains the design. Correlation in a prior scale does not by itself identify independent causal mediators.
study.dictator_results: Agency main effect is nonsignificant; patiency main effect has p .062. A real agency × patiency interaction, F(1,198) 6.26, p .013, shows the higher allocation for affective capacity is concentrated in low-agency descriptions: 3.96 versus 7.90 tickets. High-agency cell means 6.62 versus 6.06 do not show the same direction. Do not summarize a universal emotional-capacity main effect.
study.ultimatum_results: Agency and patiency main effects are reported around p .05 and .007, with no significant interaction, p .15. Adding the earlier dictator allocation as covariate gives a similar pattern. That covariate is itself post-assignment behavior, so adjustment does not remove order effects or identify an independent total effect. No direct game × manipulation comparison was reported.
study.standing_and_closeness: Mind, standing and IOS measures are collected after both simple games, not independently after each one. Standing includes protection, harm, theft, compassion/fairness and obsolete-robot questions. IOS is a single modified seven-picture overlap response. Relatedness and standing are different appraisals; neither establishes actual rights or deserved trust.
study.study_2_sample: 226 US MTurk participants, 135 men, 90 women and one undisclosed gender. After randomized descriptions and checks, they negotiate for up to six minutes. The paper excludes 78 timed-out/nonengaged cases for negotiation analyses, which would leave 148, but residual df143 in the four-cell ANOVAs imply 147 complete cases. The missing case or exclusion accounting remains unresolved.
study.study_2_manipulation: Descriptions are combined with scripted dialog, emoji responses and facial expressions. Agency includes recognizing another’s emotions; patiency is described as feeling. All agents use the same negotiation policy, but differing communication and human responses can yield different interaction histories. Emotion recognition, expression and actual feeling remain distinct.
study.negotiation_structure: Items comprise seven clocks, five records, five paintings and five lamps. Clocks/paintings have matched values across players; records/lamps have opposite priorities. This creates fixed-value distribution and potential joint-gain tradeoffs within the same task, not separate randomly assigned integrative/distributive conditions.
study.opening_offer: All agents start with the same lopsided offer, robot 40 assigned points versus human 16 with four items unallocated. The policy is described as minimax/fairness-oriented with preference-responsive adjustment. No humanlike recursive-belief implementation, optimality proof or independent fairness validation is supplied.
study.negotiation_results: Humans earn more against high-agency descriptions, about 28.825 versus 26.69; agents earn less, 34.06 versus 37.05. Joint points are nonsignificant, p .20, not proven equal. This is opposite to a simple prediction that more attributed capability improves the agent’s return, despite a constant underlying strategy.
study.process: Formal agency × patiency interactions occur for duration and rejected offers, p .02 each, especially in low-patiency conditions. High-patiency agents receive more selected happy/surprise emojis and a cooperative message. Many separate count outcomes are tested; the paper does not specify a family-wide multiplicity correction. Sent emojis are not necessarily felt emotion or calibrated cooperation.
study.post_measures: Study 2 IOS/standing analyses use residual df222, covering the larger 226-person sample rather than the active negotiation subset. Patiency is associated with closeness and standing; the printed IOS F, p and eta values are incompatible. Differences between this sample and the process subset complicate attributing all post-game appraisal differences to completed negotiation.
study.mentalizing_claim: The discussion proposes that unexpected competence causes belief revision and higher-order theory-of-mind reasoning. No repeated within-negotiation mind measure or direct recursive-belief task is reported. Longer interaction, rejecting offers and lower points do not uniquely validate that mechanism.
study.incentive_discrepancy: Study 2 instructions say the highest-scoring participant will receive $10, but the procedure says the recipient was randomly selected. Which incentive was implemented and understood needs clarification; do not silently assume identical reward contingencies.
study.scope: This is a scripted virtual-agent setting, not a modern generative negotiator, clinical intervention, actual robot feelings or proof that social appearance lacks all gender/race cues. Objective fairness need not mean an equal split under every task, and more points or greater closeness are not automatically ethical success.

summary: Add Self–other overlap and the distinct integrative/distributive bargaining approaches. Preserve conditional game findings and real interaction tests while separating actual allocations from motive, displayed emotions from feeling and closeness from trust. Record incompatible statistics, sample/incentive ambiguities and unsupported belief-update mechanisms.

findings.definition: Perceiving another person or entity as overlapping with one’s sense of self.
synonyms: Inclusion of other in the self
findings.novelty_rationale: Perceived overlap or closeness differs from trust, disclosure, shared feelings, perceived moral standing and merely inferring another’s beliefs. The appendix explicitly adapts the IOS picture scale to identification with a robot; this is not another name for any existing trust construct.

evidence.quote: describes how closely you identify with the robot

findings.evidence_scope: A single modified seven-picture IOS item is collected after both simple games and after negotiation. Assigned patiency relates to greater reported overlap; the Study 2 numeric test triplet has an unresolved inconsistency. This is a closeness appraisal, not an observed enduring relationship.
findings.boundary: Overlap ratings do not prove trust, shared values, identity fusion, healthy attachment or actual intimacy. The one-item robot adaptation does not validate equivalence to human closeness measures or machine subjective selfhood. Human rights and agency remain independent of closeness to a system.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human self-report about scripted/described agents; no subjective AI self–other representation or long-term relationship tested
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate perceived human closeness to an AI separately from warranted trust, actual disclosure and user control. Do not infer reciprocal identification from first-person language or use closeness scores as proof of safety or permission.

findings.definition: Seeking agreements that increase joint gains by trading across parties’ different priorities or interests.
findings.novelty_rationale: Creating joint value through differences in priorities is a negotiation approach, distinct from the cognitive style of integrative complexity, distributive fairness appraisal or a human-source premium. The study’s opposite record/lamp values explicitly permit such tradeoffs.

evidence.quote: the other half of items had different values
to enlarge the pie for both

findings.evidence_scope: The shared negotiation task contains integrative opportunities. The experiment varies perceived agent capacities, not integrative versus distributive strategy, and does not validate every participant’s joint-gain reasoning or a causal mentalizing mechanism.
findings.boundary: Potential joint gain does not guarantee consent, fairness, equal benefits or a feasible agreement. Relative priorities must be established rather than invented, and genuinely opposed interests can remain. Cooperation is not permission to exceed an authorized mandate.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human negotiation with a fixed scripted policy and mixed-value goods; no new AI negotiation algorithm or proven optimal policy
findings.ai_proposal: Within an authorized negotiation, identify tradeoffs using each party’s stated priorities and compare joint gains with feasible alternatives. Keep budget, rights and consent constraints explicit, and do not claim a win-win outcome without checking both parties’ values.

findings.definition: Negotiating to claim a share of a fixed amount of value.
findings.novelty_rationale: Dividing existing value is an action strategy, not a judgment that a distribution is fair and not the reasoning style integrative complexity. The study distinguishes equal-valued goods from goods with different priorities in a mixed-motive negotiation.

evidence.quote: half of the items were equally valuable to both players

findings.evidence_scope: Clocks and paintings have matched per-item values, so allocating these items changes shares without creating joint value. This structural example is not an independent experiment comparing pure bargaining strategies.
findings.boundary: A fixed-value component does not make the entire negotiation zero-sum. Claiming a share can be legitimate, but price advantage does not settle fairness or authorize deception, pressure or violating another party’s rights. Check whether integrative options remain.
findings.ai_evidence_status: A fixed-value component in a human–agent negotiation; no model-internal motive or universally effective bargaining policy demonstrated
findings.ai_proposal: Distinguish allocating a fixed resource from creating new value. Represent an authorized party’s reservation values accurately, honor agreed limits and assess distributional fairness separately from maximizing its share.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add context-dependent outcomes and measurement boundaries without treating an appraisal, displayed emotion or theoretical mechanism as the same construct.

evidence.quote: got more in the negotiation when the agent was

findings.evidence_scope: Described agency has context-dependent associations with allocations and negotiation points despite a fixed underlying agent policy. The low-agency description yields greater agent points in negotiation; process interactions with patiency are also reported.
findings.boundary: Described intelligence, perceived agency, actual policy competence, human strategic reasoning and actual machine intentions differ. Manipulated affective descriptions also shift perceived agency, so no pure independent mediator is identified.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add context-dependent outcomes and measurement boundaries without treating an appraisal, displayed emotion or theoretical mechanism as the same construct.
findings.evidence_scope: The design distinguishes recognizing human emotions from being described as able to feel. Assigned patiency changes some allocations, sent emotive messages, closeness and standing, with conditional rather than uniform economic effects.
findings.boundary: Recognition and expression do not establish subjective feeling. The joint description/dialog/expression manipulation is not a direct intervention on actual experience, and message counts do not uniquely measure participants’ felt emotions.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity a claim to moral consideration in how actions affect it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add context-dependent outcomes and measurement boundaries without treating an appraisal, displayed emotion or theoretical mechanism as the same construct.
findings.evidence_scope: Five adapted items ask about protection, harm, theft and compassion/fairness. Both description factors relate to standing after the simple-game sequence; only patiency is significant in the larger Study 2 post-measure sample.
findings.boundary: Observer standing ratings are not ethical truth or legal status. They are distinct from mind attribution and closeness, and their post-treatment timing and changing samples prevent a simple causal theory that interaction complexity makes cognition morally irrelevant.

findings.definition: Inferring another’s beliefs, intentions, desires or emotions to explain or anticipate their behavior.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add context-dependent outcomes and measurement boundaries without treating an appraisal, displayed emotion or theoretical mechanism as the same construct.

evidence.quote: Participants with low-agency agents thus applied higher theory of mind

findings.evidence_scope: The discussion interprets unexpected agent competence as encouraging greater mentalizing. The experiments do not directly test recursive beliefs or measure changing mind attributions during the interaction.
findings.boundary: Boundary-only proposed mechanism. Allocations, duration, offer rejection and final ratings do not by themselves establish higher-order reasoning, belief revision or actual AI understanding.

source_corrections.reported: The summary table lists A+P+I for moral standing after both DG and UG.
source_corrections.correction: The body reports that interaction as F(1,198) 3.65, p .06, rather than significant at .05. Mark it as uncertain/marginal, and note that standing was measured once after the two-game sequence, not as two independent findings.

source_corrections.reported: Described emotional capacity is summarized as increasing dictator-game allocations.
source_corrections.correction: Retain the main patiency p .062 and the significant agency × patiency interaction. The increase is concentrated in the low-agency cells; do not generalize it as an unconditional affective-capacity effect.
source_corrections.scope: Conditional interpretation using the source’s actual formal interaction.

source_corrections.reported: The heading calls IOS inclusion of self in other.
source_corrections.correction: Use the cited instrument’s standard name, Inclusion of Other in the Self, and preserve the actual modified instruction and seven overlap pictures.
source_corrections.scope: Instrument-name normalization, not a change to participants’ responses.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: 226 minus 78 excluded cases equals 148, whereas four-cell ANOVA residual df143 implies 147 complete cases. A missing case or an exclusion-count error could explain this, but neither is documented sufficiently to repair.

Reported F(1,222) 29.1, p .002 and partial eta-squared .04 are incompatible: that F implies eta about .116 and a much smaller p. The mean/SE pair suggests a smaller test, but exact unrounded output is unavailable. No replacement F or p invented.

Two least-used preset-message means are printed as −1.43 and −3.5 even though these are described as counts. Figure 3 explicitly standardizes game scores, not these message measures. Correct transformations or numbers require the original output; do not guess decimal repairs.
Instructions promise a bonus to the highest-scoring participant, but procedure reports random selection. No protocol or payment record was obtained to establish the implemented incentive.

The paper refers to trends reported previously in a conference publication on the same topic. Full prior paper and participant overlap were not checked; do not count it as a second independent replication or infer separate samples from another citation alone.

Only one targeted author-encoding correction was verified before a metadata rate limit. Other chapter/editor fields and missing conference details remain unverified; no exhaustive bibliography audit is claimed.

methodological_limits: The studies directly measure ticket allocations, game points and selected messages alongside subjective appraisals. They do not directly measure moral motives, recursive beliefs, emotion experience or rights.

Game order is fixed and some measures occur only once after both games. Post-assignment dictator allocations are not a neutral pretreatment covariate for ultimatum behavior. Separate tests and standardized plots do not provide a formal cross-task interaction.

Agency and patiency manipulations cross-affect perceptions and bundle descriptions with expressions/dialogs. A clean factorial assignment does not mean independent perceived psychological dimensions or unique mediators.

A fixed negotiation policy does not imply identical offers throughout adaptive conversations. Appearance lacks explicitly assigned gender/race labels, but absence of all social cues was not independently validated.

Negotiation outcome/process analyses use a smaller and incompletely reconciled engagement subset, while IOS/standing tests use the larger sample. Do not treat all reported endpoints as the same 226 completed negotiations.

Many selected message/emoji counts are analyzed separately without an explicit family-wide correction. Negative raw count means and inconsistent IOS test values need output verification before quantitative reuse.

Higher joint points can be consistent with effective tradeoffs without uniquely identifying higher-order mentalizing. No significant joint-score difference does not prove identical outcomes, no cognitive process or absence of effect.

Greater standing, closeness or willingness to allocate is not calibrated trust, actual sentience or a universal ethical obligation. Equal division is one possible fairness rule, not the sole justified criterion in every negotiation.
No participant data, original implementation, saved statistics or prior conference sample were inspected. Three new concepts are clearly separated from the paper’s untested causal explanations.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Agency/experience items and task contexts can produce different patterns. Perceived capacity is not actual mental status, and repeated allocations are not independent people.
Distributive fairness appraisal is distinct from distributing value or obtaining a favorable outcome. Different dependent variables require their own evidence.
Task-specific agent choices can differ from expected-proficiency ratings. A behavioral pattern alone does not identify an unconscious stereotype or a unique mentalizing mechanism.
Actual disclosure, willingness, trust and liking differ. Here closeness and standing add further distinct appraisals; post-treatment scores cannot prove reciprocal feeling or a causal change process.

deferred.term: Higher-order belief revision as another newly demonstrated behavior
deferred.reason: The paper proposes this explanation but does not directly measure nested belief reasoning or changing attributions over negotiation time. Retain it as a boundary in existing mentalizing.

deferred.term: Emotion recognition as actual machine feeling
deferred.reason: Recognition, expression and experience are explicitly distinguished in the paper. Scripted responses are not subjective affect.

deferred.term: Low-agency negotiation advantage as a universal new bias
deferred.reason: A context-specific outcome contrast with an identical policy does not establish one general motive or stable mechanism. Preserve it in existing agency-attribution evidence.

limitations: Three new constructs/approaches. Existing stable IDs and eleven categories preserved; no forced citation quota, invented yearly totals, automatic ethical/harm edges or full-paper Markdown transcription.
